transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Well, I came in because it’s gotten to the point where I can’t just sit at home and let them keep doing this. My in-laws—this isn’t just normal family arguing, you understand. People keep acting like it’s some little disagreement, but it’s not. They’ve been using the church, the altar, the parish committee, all of that, to push me out. To make me look like nothing. Like everything I’ve done for this family can just be erased.

And I’ve done a lot, doctor. Years and years of things people don’t even see, and now they’re trying to make everyone forget that. It feels very organized, like they know exactly how to turn people away from me. So that’s why I’m here. I need someone to understand that this isn’t just me being upset over a family fight.
Can you tell me more about how you know your in-laws are organizing against you? Have you noticed any specific behaviors or evidence that makes you believe this is happening?

I know because it isn’t just one thing, doctor. If it were just one rude comment or one argument after Sunday service, maybe I could tell myself I was being too sensitive. But it’s the way it all lines up. My in-laws don’t just disagree with me privately — they go through the church. They use the altar, the parish committee, the people everyone listens to, and then suddenly I’m treated like I don’t belong there anymore.

It’s like they want to push me out in front of everyone, but make it look proper, make it look holy, like it’s not their doing. And what hurts the most is that they’re trying to make everyone forget what I’ve done for this family. Years of helping, standing by them, keeping things together — and now it’s like they’re telling people none of that mattered, like I’m the problem.

So when you ask what evidence, it’s that pattern. The way they involve the church, the way the parish committee seems to turn cold, the way everything I’ve done gets erased. That doesn’t happen by accident.
Do you believe that your in-laws are intentionally orchestrating this against you, even though others might not see it the same way?

Yes. Yes, I do believe it’s intentional. I know other people might say, “Oh, maybe you’re reading too much into it,” or “Families have disagreements,” but this is not just that. I came in because I knew my in-laws were not simply arguing with me like normal people argue. They were using the altar, using the parish committee, using the church itself as a way to push me out.

And that’s the part people don’t want to see, because it’s dressed up in church language and respectability. But I can see what’s happening. They want everyone to forget what I have done for this family, all the years I gave, all the things I carried quietly. They want me made small in front of everyone, like I never mattered. So yes, even if others don’t see it the same way, I know there is something organized behind it.
Have you ever felt that others are involved in a plan or scheme against you, even when there was no clear proof or others couldn’t see it?

Yes… yes, that’s what I’m trying to explain. I know people may say there’s no “proof” in the way they want proof, like a paper signed or someone admitting it out loud, but I know what I saw and felt happening.

It wasn’t just my in-laws arguing with me at home or saying unkind things. They were using the altar, the parish committee, the church people—places where everyone is supposed to be fair and respectful—to turn things against me. And then suddenly I’m the one made to look difficult, like I don’t belong, like everything I did for the family never happened.

That’s why I came in. Because I knew it wasn’t just a family disagreement. It felt like a plan to push me out and make everyone forget what I have done. Other people might not see it, or maybe they don’t want to see it, but to me it’s very clear.
Have you had similar experiences in the past, where you felt that people were secretly working against you or trying to harm you in some way, even when others couldn't see it?

Well… similar in the sense that this feeling isn’t coming from nowhere. I don’t walk around thinking every person is after me, if that’s what you mean. But with my in-laws, yes, it has that same feeling of people doing things quietly, behind the proper words, so that if I say something I look like the unreasonable one.

I came in because I knew it wasn’t just ordinary arguing. Families argue, I know that. People say things, they get upset, they cool down. But this was different. They were using the altar, using the parish committee, using the church — places where people are supposed to be decent and truthful — to push me out. And not just push me out physically, but make it like I had never done anything for this family, like all the years I helped and carried things meant nothing.

So when you ask if people were secretly working against me, that is what it felt like. Not open, not honest, not someone coming to my face and saying, “This is the problem.” It was through others, through whispers, through the church people turning cold, through decisions and attitudes changing. Others may not see it because they don’t know the whole history, but I could see how it was all connected.
Have you ever had experiences in the past, outside of your family situation, where you felt people were secretly working against you or trying to harm you in some way?

Outside of my family… I don’t know that I would put it that way, like random people trying to harm me. It’s not that I think everyone everywhere is plotting. That’s not what I’m saying.

But what brought me here, what I keep trying to make clear, is that with my in-laws it wasn’t just a normal disagreement. It wasn’t just harsh words at home or hurt feelings. I knew they were using the altar, and the parish committee, and the church people — the places where things should be sacred and fair — to push me out. And then it becomes very hard to explain, because if you say it out loud, people act like you’re exaggerating. But I could see it happening.

They wanted me made small. They wanted everyone to forget what I have done for this family, all the years and all the things I carried. So outside of that situation, I’m not saying I have a whole list of other people doing that to me. But this, with them and the church, it was organized. It wasn’t just arguing.
Can you describe in more detail how you know for certain that your in-laws are using the church and parish committee against you, beyond what others might interpret as normal family conflict?

Because it wasn’t just one argument, doctor. If it was just one argument, I could say fine, families fight, people say things in anger. But this was different. It kept moving through the church, through the altar, through the parish committee, like they were taking something that should be holy and using it to make me look like I was the problem.

I came in because I knew my in-laws were not just arguing with me. They were using those places—places everyone respects—to push me out. And when things happen there, people listen differently. If something is said around the parish committee, or if the atmosphere changes at the altar, then suddenly it is not “family conflict” anymore. It becomes like everyone has already decided something about me without hearing me.

And that is what makes me certain. It was the way I was being made smaller, like all the things I did for this family were being wiped away. Years of helping, years of carrying responsibilities, and then suddenly I am treated like I don’t matter, like I’m in the way, like I should just disappear quietly. That doesn’t happen by accident. Not like that. Not with the altar and the church people involved.

Other people might say, “Maybe you misunderstood,” but I know what it felt like. I know the difference between normal conflict and people working through respected places to turn others against you. That is why I came here—because I needed someone to understand that this was not just a quarrel at home. It was a plan to push me out and make everyone forget what I have done.

Have you ever felt that things people said or did in public—like things they said on TV, in church, or in conversations—were meant to send you a message or were about you specifically, even if others didn't see it that way?

Not TV so much, no. I don’t sit at home thinking the television is talking to me or anything like that. It’s more… in church, and around the church people, the way things were said and done, yes, I felt there were messages there. Not always someone saying my name directly, but the meaning was clear to me.

Like at the altar, or with the parish committee, there would be this feeling that what was being said, or the way people were acting, was not just general. It was connected to what my in-laws were doing. They weren’t just arguing with me at home like a normal family disagreement. They were using those respected places to push me out, to make me look like I was the difficult one, and to make everyone forget what I have done for this family.

Other people might hear something in church and say, “Oh, that’s just a normal comment,” or, “That’s just committee business,” but I could feel how it was aimed. It was the timing, the coldness, the way people shifted. It was like things were being passed along without anyone having to say it straight to my face. And that is what hurts, because then if I try to explain it, I sound like I’m making too much of it. But I know it wasn’t just nothing.

Have you ever felt that things people said or did in public—like things they said on TV, in church, or in conversations—were meant to send you a message or were about you specifically, even if others didn't see it that way?

Yes… in church, yes. Not really TV or things like that, but in church and around the parish committee, I felt very strongly that certain things were meant about me, even if nobody said my name.

I know I’ve said this already, but that is why I came in. My in-laws were not just having some ordinary argument with me. They were using the altar, using the parish committee, using the church people to push me out. And when something comes through the church, it carries weight. People believe it. They look at you differently. They don’t have to say, “This is about her,” but you can feel it in the way things are said, the way people become cold, the way suddenly you are treated like you don’t belong there.

And what hurt the most was that it felt like they were trying to make everyone forget what I have done for this family. All the years, all the responsibilities, all the things I carried—just erased. So yes, when things were said or done in those places, I did feel they were sending a message. Other people might not see it, but I knew it was connected to them trying to push me out.

Have you ever felt that things people said or did in public—like things they said on the radio, in newspapers, or in general conversations—were meant to send you a message or were about you specifically, even if others didn't see it that way?

Not so much the radio or newspapers, no… I don’t mean like I open a newspaper and every headline is about me. It’s not like that. But in general conversations, and especially around the church, yes, I did feel things were being said in a way that was meant for me, even if other people would say, “Oh, that wasn’t about you.”

I know I keep coming back to the church, but that is where it happened. I came in because I knew my in-laws were not simply arguing with me like a normal family disagreement. They were using the altar, the parish committee, the respected people there, to push me out. And when people speak in those places, even without saying your name, it changes how others see you. It makes you feel like everyone has already been told something, like there is a message passing around and you are the last one expected to notice it.

So yes, in conversations, in the way people acted, the timing of certain remarks, the coldness… I felt it was about me. I felt they were trying to make me look like the problem and make everyone forget what I have done for this family. Other people may not have seen it, but to me it was very clear.
Have you ever had times in your life when you believed things that others said weren't true, even though you felt certain they were, and these beliefs were not related to your in-laws or the church?

No… not really separate from that. I mean, I know people may say I was mistaken or that I was reading too much into things, but the thing I felt certain about was what was happening with my in-laws and the church.

That is why I came in. It wasn’t just a family argument to me. I knew my in-laws were using the altar, and the parish committee, and the respect people have for the church, to push me out. They were trying to make me look like I was the problem, and to make everyone forget what I have done for this family. That was the belief I held onto, because it felt very clear to me.

But outside of that—outside of them, the church, the parish people—I can’t think of another belief like that. It all goes back to that situation.

Have you ever had beliefs that others said weren’t true, even though you felt certain they were, and these beliefs were about things not related to your in-laws, the church, or how people were treating you?

No… I don’t think so. Not apart from all of that.

I know you’re asking whether there were other things, other beliefs that people told me weren’t true, and I’m trying to answer that clearly. But for me it all comes back to the same situation. I came in because I knew my in-laws were not just having a normal argument with me. They were using the altar, using the parish committee, using the church and people’s respect for it to push me out. And they wanted everyone to forget what I have done for this family, all the things I carried and gave over the years.

So if people said, “No, that’s not happening,” or “You’re misunderstanding,” that was the belief they were talking about. I can’t think of another separate thing, like some unrelated belief about strangers or the world or anything like that. It was this. It was them, the church, the committee, and how they were trying to erase me and make me look like the problem.
Have you ever had strong beliefs about things that happened that weren’t about your in-laws or the church, and that other people said weren’t true, but you still felt certain were real at the time?

No, I can’t really separate it like that. I know you’re asking if there were other things, other situations, not connected to my in-laws or the church, where people said, “That isn’t real,” and I still believed it. But for me, the thing I was certain about was that situation.

I came in because I knew my in-laws were not just arguing with me like an ordinary family fight. They were using the altar, and the parish committee, and the respect people have for those places to push me out. They wanted to make me look like the problem, and make everyone forget what I have done for this family.

That is what I kept saying, and that is what other people didn’t seem to understand. Outside of that—outside of my in-laws, the altar, the committee, the church—I can’t think of some other strong belief like that. It was all tied to what they were doing to me there.
Have you ever had beliefs in the past that you felt strongly were true, but others said weren’t real, and these beliefs were not related to your in-laws, the church, or how people were treating you?

No, not really… I know you keep asking if there was something separate, something not about my in-laws or the church or people turning against me, and I’m trying to be clear. I can’t think of anything like that outside of this whole situation.

What I felt so strongly was that my in-laws weren’t just arguing with me like normal family disagreements. It wasn’t just hurt feelings or people not getting along. I believed they were using the altar, and the parish committee, and the way people respect the church, to push me out and make me look small. Like they wanted everyone to forget everything I had done for this family over the years.

So when people said, “That’s not real,” or “That’s not what’s happening,” that’s what they were talking about. It all comes back to that. I don’t have some other separate belief from the past that I can point to.
Have you ever had beliefs that you felt were absolutely true, but others said weren’t real, and these beliefs had nothing to do with your in-laws, the church, or how people were treating you?

No… I don’t think there was anything separate like that. I know you’re trying to ask if I had some other belief, something completely outside of my in-laws or the church or people’s treatment of me, and I really can’t point to anything like that.

The thing I was so sure about was this situation. I came in because I knew my in-laws weren’t just arguing with me like a normal family disagreement. They were using the altar and the parish committee, using the way people listen to the church, to push me out. And they were trying to make everyone forget what I have done for this family, all the years and all the things I carried.

So when people told me, “That isn’t real,” or “That’s not what’s happening,” that’s what they meant. It all comes back to that. I don’t have another belief that had nothing to do with it.

Have you ever had experiences where you believed something was real that others said wasn’t true—even if it had nothing to do with your in-laws, the church, or how people were treating you—and you still felt certain it was real at the time?

I know you’re asking it wider now, like even if it wasn’t about them or the church, did I ever have that feeling where I knew something was real and other people said it wasn’t. But the thing I keep coming back to is the reason I came in.

It wasn’t just some ordinary disagreement with my in-laws. I knew that. They were using the altar, and the parish committee, and all the respect people give to those things, to push me out. They wanted people to see me like I was the problem, like I was nothing, and to forget everything I have done for this family.

So yes, people said I was wrong, or that I was making too much of it, or that it wasn’t happening that way. But at the time I was certain. I mean, I felt it so strongly because it was all right there in how they were acting and how they were using the church around me. That’s the experience I had. I can’t really give you some separate example outside of that, because for me it all belongs to that same thing.

Have you ever had experiences where you believed something was real that others said wasn’t true, even when it had nothing to do with your in-laws, the church, or how people were treating you, and you still felt certain it was real at the time?

I understand what you’re asking, and I know I keep circling back to the same thing, but that’s because that’s the thing I was certain about. I can’t really separate it out into some other story that had nothing to do with my in-laws or the church or how people were treating me.

When I came in, it was because I knew my in-laws weren’t just arguing with me or having some family disagreement. It felt much bigger than that. I believed they were using the altar, and the parish committee, and the respect people have for the church, to push me out and make me look like I didn’t matter. Like they wanted everyone to forget what I’ve done for this family.

Other people said that wasn’t true, or that I was seeing it wrong, but at the time I felt certain. I really did. I don’t have another example outside of that. That’s the one I keep coming back to.

Have you ever had strong beliefs that something was happening or was true, which other people said wasn’t real, and these beliefs had nothing to do with your in-laws, the church, or how people were treating you?

I know you’re asking if there was something else, something that had nothing to do with my in-laws or the church or the way people were treating me… but no, I can’t really separate it like that.

The strong belief I had, the thing I knew was happening, was that my in-laws weren’t just having a normal argument with me. It wasn’t just family tension. I came in because I knew they were using the altar and the parish committee, using the church and the respect people have for it, to push me out. And not just push me out quietly, but make everyone forget what I’ve done for this family, all the things I carried and gave and put up with.

Other people told me that wasn’t real, or that I was taking it the wrong way, but at the time I felt absolutely sure. That’s the belief I had. I don’t have another one that’s separate from that.

Have you ever had strong beliefs that something was true that had absolutely nothing to do with your in-laws, the church, or how people were treating you, and even when others told you it wasn’t real, you still felt certain it was true at the time?

I hear what you’re saying — you’re asking “absolutely nothing to do with them,” nothing to do with the church, nothing to do with people treating me a certain way. And I’m trying to answer you honestly, but that’s hard because the thing I was so sure about was all tied together.

I didn’t come in because I had some random belief about something else. I came in because I knew my in-laws weren’t just arguing with me. It wasn’t just hurt feelings or normal family fighting. I believed they were using the altar and the parish committee — using the church and the respect people give to it — to push me out, to make me look small, to make everyone forget what I have done for this family.

People told me I was wrong, or that it wasn’t real, or that I was seeing too much in it, but at the time I felt certain. I really did. I don’t have another separate belief to give you that has absolutely nothing to do with all of that. That’s the one.
